chunks.section: Rethinking LoRA Initialization for Robust Asymmetric Learning Rates
chunks.text: Disen Liao Affiliation: University of Waterloo Affiliation: Vector Institute Email: d7liao@uwaterloo.ca Yaoliang Yu Affiliation: University of Waterloo Affiliation: Vector Institute Email: yaoliang.yu@uwaterloo.ca

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix B B than for the down-projection matrix A A . However, the ratio η B / η A \eta_{B}/\eta_{A} itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal–noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. Under standard Init[A] , the update contains an initialization-induced noise term whose magnitude can be affected by the LR for B B , η B \eta_{B} , the initialization scale β \beta , and the adapter rank r r . In practical LLM fine-tuning, this non-vanishing noise can limit the performance gains expected from LoRA+ style asymmetric LRs. To suppress this effect, we propose Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] , a simple initialization that scales the variance of A A as σ A 2 ∝ n − 2 \sigma_{A}^{2}\propto n^{-2} while keeping B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 . Under matched rank and training time for both initializations, this reduces the initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of 1 / n 1/n , stabilizing asymmetric LoRA training while preserving zero initial adapter output. Empirically, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] substantially widens the stable LR region across initialization scales, adapter ranks, and LoRA update multipliers. Across tasks and models, Init[ A

apter output. Empirically, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] substantially widens the stable LR region across initialization scales, adapter ranks, and LoRA update multipliers. Across tasks and models, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] reduces best-ratio drift, prevents the high-ratio collapse observed with standard Init[A] , and makes the width-based guideline η B ≈ n ​ η A \eta_{B}\approx n\eta_{A} a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 22 ] is a standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) [ 21 , 35 , 33 ] . Given a width- n n LoRA layer with pretrained weight W ∈ ℝ n × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and input Z ¯ ∈ ℝ n \underline{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , LoRA uses Z ¯ = W ​ Z ¯ + α r ​ B ​ A ​ Z ¯ \bar{Z}=W\underline{Z}+\frac{\alpha}{r}BA\underline{Z} , where A ∈ ℝ r × n A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} and B ∈ ℝ n × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} are trainable with learning rates (LRs) η A \eta_{A} and η B \eta_{B} . Here r ≪ n r\ll n is the adapter rank and α / r \alpha/r is the LoRA update multiplier. We use β \beta to denote the initialization-magnitude hyperparameter: standard LoRA initialization, denoted Init[A] , initializes B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 and initializes A 0 A_{0} randomly with mean zero and standard deviation β n − 1 / 2 \beta n^{-1/2} , so the adapter preserves the pretrained model output at step zero. Figure 1 : Overview of LoRA initialization and feature-norm stability. Left : LoRA branch notation and the initialization scalings compared in this work, including standard Init[A] , Init[AB] , and the proposed Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] . Right : feature-norm trajectories at width n = 4096 n=4096 for different initialization scales β \beta . Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] keeps the LoRA features nearly invariant to β \beta , while the alternative scalings exhibit stronger initialization-dependent growth.

Despite its simplicity, LoRA is sensitive to hyperparameters (HPs). The rank r r controls the expressive capacity of the adapter [ 60 ] , but its effect is inseparable from the update multiplier λ r = α / r \lambda_{r}=\alpha/r . Kalajdzievski [ 27 ] shows that the conventional choice α / r \alpha/r is not rank-stabilized: it can shrink adapter activations and gradients as r r grows, slowing learning at high ranks and motivating the alternative α / r \alpha/\sqrt{r} . LRs introduce a further source of brittleness. Recent empirical work shows that, after sufficiently broad LR sweeps, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants [ 32 ] . This shifts the practical question from only designing new adapters to understanding LoRA HP selection. LoRA+ [ 17 ] gives a principled route toward understanding LR selection by assigning different LRs to the two LoRA matrices. Its infinite-width feature learning analysis suggests that efficient LoRA feature updates require an asymmetric regime with η B ≫ η A \eta_{B}\gg\eta_{A} and, under idealized scaling assumptions, a ratio η B / η A ≈ n \eta_{B}/\eta_{A}\approx n . We write this ratio as ρ = η B / η A \rho=\eta_{B}/\eta_{A} . The asymmetric regime is attractive because B B directly controls the LoRA branch output, so increasing η B \eta_{B} can accelerate adaptation. In finite pretrained LLMs, however, ρ \rho often becomes another hyperparameter to tune: large ratios can improve performance, but under Init[A] they can also trigger instability. We address the gap between the theoretical LR guidance and practical LLM fine-tuning in this paper.

We show that the fragility of asymmetric LRs comes from an initialization-dependent noise term that survives even though the LoRA branch has zero output at initialization. Although B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 , the random matrix A 0 A_{0} affects the branch as soon as B B moves away from zero. A signal–noise decomposition of the LoRA feature update reveals two components: a task-driven signal from optimizer updates and a noise term from the interaction between the learned B B and the random initial A A . Both terms scale with η B \eta_{B} , so increasing η B \eta_{B} amplifies useful adaptation and initialization noise at the same time. In the small-LR regime common in pretrained LLM fine-tuning, the signal can remain controlled while the Init[A] noise contribution does not vanish with width, making large ρ \rho , large initialization scale β \beta , and large update multiplier α / r \alpha/r especially brittle.

We propose Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] , a minimal initialization change that suppresses this noise at its source. 1 1 1 Our code is available at https://github.com/liaodisen/LoRA-initA2 . Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] keeps the standard zero initialization for B B , but initializes A A with one additional factor of width scaling: instead of σ A 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \sigma_{A}^{2}=\Theta(n^{-1}) , it uses σ A 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n − 2 ) \sigma_{A}^{2}=\Theta(n^{-2}) . This preserves the LoRA architecture, training objective, and zero initial adapter output. The purpose is not to make the adapter inactive, but to prevent the random initial projection from being amplified by η B \eta_{B} , α / r \alpha/r , or β \beta before a task-driven signal has formed. For comparable rank and time scaling of the optimizer updates, this reduces the initialization-noise energy by a factor of 1 / n 1/n . We do not claim that ρ = n \rho=n is always the finite-model optimum; instead, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] reduces the need for exhaustive two-dimensional LR search by making the high-ratio regime substantially more stable. We validate this claim through LR sweeps and fine-tuning experiments. On a controlled toy problem, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] improves hyperparameter transfer across widths and keeps internal and output LoRA feature norms stable as β \beta grows. On encoder-only RoBERTa fine-tuning and decoder-only arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] preserves the benefit of η B > η A \eta_{B}>\eta_{A} while widening the stable LR region and reducing best-ratio drift. These results position Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] as a lightweight initialization rule for making LoRA+-style asymmetric LR tuning practical in finite pretrained models. Our contributions are threefold:

• We identify an LR-ratio failure mode in LoRA: asymmetric LRs with η B > η A \eta_{B}>\eta_{A} can improve adaptation, but under standard Init[A] the ratio ρ \rho becomes brittle because η B \eta_{B} amplifies both the useful signal and an initialization-dependent noise term. • We introduce Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] , a simple LoRA initialization rule that sets σ A 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n − 2 ) \sigma_{A}^{2}=\Theta(n^{-2}) while keeping B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 . It preserves the feature-learning property of standard Init[A] under the same asymmetric LR scaling, while suppressing the initialization-noise term without changing the LoRA architecture, objective, zero-output initialization, or training cost. • We show theoretically and empirically that Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] widens the stable LR region, improves robustness to large initialization scales and LoRA update multipliers, and makes asymmetric LR selection more predictable across models and tasks.

chunks.section: 2.2 Prior Work on LoRA with Scaling Theory
chunks.text: The theoretical analysis of deep neural networks is often impeded by nonlinearities and high-dimensional interactions. To make the behavior tractable, prior work often studies these models in infinite-width or infinite-depth limits, leveraging asymptotic properties governed by the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and the Law of Large Numbers (LLN), reviewed in Section A.1 . A critical objective within this framework is to identify scaling laws that avoid the “lazy” kernel regime, thereby preserving the model’s ability to perform nontrivial feature learning [ 56 ] as dimensions grow. This scaling-limit perspective has facilitated the derivation of feature-preserving HP transfer rules for Transformers [ 55 , 14 ] and Residual Networks [ 7 , 58 ] , as well as the analysis of low-precision training stability [ 6 ] . More recently, these techniques have been adapted to the analysis of LoRA, offering insights into initialization schemes and LR scalings that support feature adaptation [ 18 , 17 , 34 ] . We discuss more related work in Appendix B .

To derive optimal scaling rules, Hayou et al. [17] analyze the fine-tuning process through a coordinate-wise feature learning perspective. When α / r = 1 \alpha/r=1 , the update Δ ​ Z B t := Z B t + 1 − Z B t \Delta Z_{B}^{t}:=Z_{B}^{t+1}-Z_{B}^{t} decomposes into three interaction terms, where Δ ​ Z A t := Z A t + 1 − Z A t \Delta Z_{A}^{t}:=Z_{A}^{t+1}-Z_{A}^{t} : Δ ​ Z B t = B t ​ Δ ​ Z A t ⏟ δ 1 t + Δ ​ B t ​ Z A t ⏟ δ 2 t + Δ ​ B t ​ Δ ​ Z A t ⏟ δ 3 t . \Delta Z_{B}^{t}=\underbrace{B_{t}\Delta Z_{A}^{t}}_{\delta_{1}^{t}}+\underbrace{\Delta B_{t}Z_{A}^{t}}_{\delta_{2}^{t}}+\underbrace{\Delta B_{t}\Delta Z_{A}^{t}}_{\delta_{3}^{t}}. (2)

Hayou et al. [17] propose two conditions on this update: 1. Stability: for all t > 1 t>1 , Z B t Z_{B}^{t} has Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \Theta(1) coordinate size as the width n → ∞ n\rightarrow\infty . 2. Efficiency: for all t > 1 t>1 , both δ 1 t \delta_{1}^{t} and δ 2 t \delta_{2}^{t} have Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \Theta(1) coordinate size as the width n → ∞ n\rightarrow\infty . To systematically analyze these constraints, Hayou et al. [17] employ the γ \gamma -calculus, which quantifies the scaling of a variable v v : if v = Θ ⁡ ( n λ ) v=\Theta(n^{\lambda}) , then γ ⁡ [ v ] = λ \gamma[v]=\lambda . For a matrix or vector X X , γ ⁡ [ X ] = λ \gamma[X]=\lambda means that each coordinate scales as Θ ⁡ ( n λ ) \Theta(n^{\lambda}) (see Section A.2 for details). By applying this framework to Condition 1 , Hayou et al. [17] demonstrate that standard symmetric LRs cannot satisfy both stability and efficiency simultaneously. Consequently, they advocate for asymmetric configurations, specifically Init[A] ( B 0 = 0 , σ A 2 = Θ ⁡ ( 1 / n ) B_{0}=0,\sigma_{A}^{2}=\Theta(1/n) ) paired with η A = Θ ⁡ ( 1 / n ) \eta_{A}=\Theta(1/n) and η B = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \eta_{B}=\Theta(1) . Using a similar γ \gamma -calculus analysis under the equal-LR setting (i.e., η A = η B = η ∗ \eta_{A}=\eta_{B}=\eta^{*} ), Hayou et al. [18] show that Init[A] is better than Init[B] because it can tolerate a larger LR. Based on related analysis, Li et al. [34] challenge the necessity of zero initialization. Introducing the concept of robustness , they investigate whether initialization can preserve stability even when HPs deviate from optimal γ \gamma -scales. Their findings suggest that fine-tuning is more stable under η A = η B \eta_{A}=\eta_{B} when both matrices are initialized nonzero (i.e., Init[AB] ).

Previous work analyzes LoRA through a feature learning perspective, but achieving feature learning can be challenging in practice. Although Hayou et al. [17] propose the scaling η B ≫ η A \eta_{B}\gg\eta_{A} , the best ratio for a finite model still requires costly tuning. Furthermore, practical deployments may use a large LoRA update multiplier α / r \alpha/r to encourage rapid adaptation, even when LRs are small. In this section, we show that standard Init[A] then has initialization-induced noise that can accumulate over training, whereas our proposed Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] suppresses this source of instability.

We consider the LoRA setup defined in Equation 1 . We explicitly parameterize the initialization magnitude using a scalar β \beta . Let A ~ 0 \tilde{A}_{0} be a base initialization matrix with entries i.i.d. 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ A 2 ) \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{A}^{2}) . The trainable matrices are initialized as B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 and A 0 = β ​ A ~ 0 A_{0}=\beta\tilde{A}_{0} .

We separate the scalar LR scale from the matrix-valued optimizer direction. Specifically, let U A t ∈ ℝ r × n U_{A}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} and U B t ∈ ℝ n × r U_{B}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} denote the directions produced by the optimizer at step t t , after any coordinate-wise normalization or adaptive preconditioning but before multiplication by the LoRA-specific LRs: A t + 1 = A t − η A ​ U A t , B t + 1 = B t − η B ​ U B t , A_{t+1}=A_{t}-\eta_{A}U_{A}^{t},\qquad B_{t+1}=B_{t}-\eta_{B}U_{B}^{t}, where the entries of U A t U_{A}^{t} and U B t U_{B}^{t} have coordinate size O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) uniformly in the width n n . This formulation abstracts away the optimizer-specific normalization while keeping the LoRA-specific LR scale explicit. The algebraic identities derived below ( Lemma 1 ) hold for any realized sequence of such update directions; optimizer-specific assumptions are needed only when estimating their scaling with width. SignSGD is the special case U = sign ⁡ ( ∇ ℒ ) U=\operatorname{sign}(\nabla\mathcal{L}) , while Adam and AdamW also fit this normalized-direction model under the non-degeneracy conditions given in Section A.4 .

We make an assumption on the alignment between block A A update and input Z ¯ \underline{Z} following the LoRA+ analysis [ 17 ] . To see this, for a single token trained with loss ℒ \mathcal{L} : ∇ A ℒ t = α r ​ B t ⊤ ​ d ​ Z ¯ t ​ Z ¯ ⊤ , \nabla_{A}\mathcal{L}_{t}=\frac{\alpha}{r}B_{t}^{\top}d\bar{Z}_{t}\,\underline{Z}^{\top}, so each row of the A A -gradient is a scalar multiplication of the input. We therefore assume optimizer normalization preserves this input coupling: | ( U A t ) i , : Z ¯ | = Θ ( n ) , i ∈ [ r ] . |(U_{A}^{t})_{i,:}\underline{Z}|=\Theta(n),\qquad i\in[r]. Sufficient conditions for SignSGD, Adam, and AdamW are given in Section A.4 . However, this condition is not generally held in the minibatch setting, the measured minibatch alignment in Sections A.4.6 and 8 varies by module and training stage, so this condition is not asserted generically for minibatch fine-tuning. Using these update equations, we can unroll A t A_{t} and B t B_{t} and separate the contribution of the random initialization A 0 A_{0} (noise) from that of the accumulated optimizer updates in both LoRA factors (signal). The following lemma gives exact decompositions of both the LoRA feature and its one-step update. The alignment condition above is not needed for the decomposition itself and enters only in the subsequent scaling analysis.

To compare their magnitudes across model widths and training time, we consider the width-normalized squared Euclidean norm E total t := 1 n ​ ‖ Z B t ‖ 2 2 E_{\text{total}}^{t}:=\frac{1}{n}\|Z_{B}^{t}\|_{2}^{2} , which is the mean squared magnitude per output coordinate. We refer to this quantity as feature energy. It can be decomposed into three terms:

E total t = E N t + E S t + E X t . E_{\text{total}}^{t}=E_{N}^{t}+E_{S}^{t}+E_{X}^{t}. Curves show the RMS magnitudes E N t \sqrt{E_{N}^{t}} (noise), E S t \sqrt{E_{S}^{t}} (signal), and E total t \sqrt{E_{\text{total}}^{t}} (total). We aim to keep the LoRA feature Z B Z_{B} bounded as training progresses. To define this form of robustness, we first choose a scaling for the training horizon T ⁡ ( n ) T(n) as a function of model width n n . According to the neural scaling laws derived by Kaplan et al. [28] , optimal training steps S S scale very weakly with model size. Specifically, they find S ∝ C min 0.03 S\propto C_{\min}^{0.03} and N param ∝ C min 0.73 N_{\text{param}}\propto C_{\min}^{0.73} , for some fixed efficient computation budget C min C_{\min} , which implies S ∝ N param 0.04 S\propto N_{\text{param}}^{0.04} . Since the parameter count N param N_{\text{param}} scales quadratically with width ( N param ∝ n 2 N_{\text{param}}\propto n^{2} ), the training steps scale as S ∝ n 0.08 S\propto n^{0.08} . Even under less optimal, fixed-compute regimes, training horizons grow sub-linearly. This motivates studying sub- n \sqrt{n} horizons, but we do not claim that the pretraining scaling will directly determine the fine-tuning schedules. Thus, we assume the training horizon satisfies T ⁡ ( n ) = o ⁡ ( n ) T(n)=o(\sqrt{n}) .

Then E N t = Θ ⁡ ( η B 2 ​ β 2 ​ m N 2 ​ σ A 2 ​ n ​ t 2 ) , E S t = Θ ⁡ ( ( η A ​ η B ​ m S ​ n ​ t 2 ) 2 ) . E_{N}^{t}=\Theta(\eta_{B}^{2}\beta^{2}m_{N}^{2}\sigma_{A}^{2}nt^{2}),\qquad E_{S}^{t}=\Theta((\eta_{A}\eta_{B}m_{S}nt^{2})^{2}). The full statement and proof are in Section A.3 .

The exponents γ N , γ S \gamma_{N},\gamma_{S} describe realized rank contraction for C t ​ u C_{t}u and C t ​ v t C_{t}v_{t} , respectively: γ = 1 \gamma=1 is coherent, LLN-like scaling and γ = 1 / 2 \gamma=1/2 is CLT-like scaling, without asserting either probabilistic limit law. The noise and signal need not share an exponent. The explicit factors of t t are separate temporal-accumulation assumptions, not consequences of rank coherence or per-step alignment. The probe measurements in Figure 7 motivate model- and stage-dependent exponents but do not verify these accumulated contractions. At fixed rank and α / r = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \alpha/r=\Theta(1) , both m N , m S = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) m_{N},m_{S}=\Theta(1) , preserving the width comparison. When rank varies, the energy ratio also contains r 2 ​ ( γ N − γ S ) r^{2(\gamma_{N}-\gamma_{S})} . For fixed rank, α / r = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \alpha/r=\Theta(1) , and finite time, practitioners often take η A ​ η B ≪ n − 1 \eta_{A}\eta_{B}\ll n^{-1} to keep the signal small under the stated assumptions. Standard Init[A] nevertheless leaves a persistent initialization-dependent component because σ A 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \sigma_{A}^{2}=\Theta(n^{-1}) : E N , Init[A] t = Θ ⁡ ( η B 2 ​ β 2 ​ m N 2 ​ t 2 ) . At fixed α / r \alpha/r , its rank factor is r 2 ​ γ N r^{2\gamma_{N}} : r 2 r^{2} for LLN-like contraction and r r for CLT-like contraction. Because η B \eta_{B} multiplies both components, the LR for block B B controls their common scale. We examine this by freezing block A A and sweeping only η B \eta_{B} in Sections D.2 and 10 . Nor does it imply a 1 / n 1/n reduction in total energy: when E N t / E S t → 0 E_{N}^{t}/E_{S}^{t}\to 0 , the total becomes signal-dominated. chunks.section: 3.3 Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] Still Enables Feature Learning
chunks.text: Having established conditions for suppressing initialization noise and controlling feature energy, we next verify that Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] still supports nontrivial feature learning, which underlies HP transfer [ 55 ] and LoRA rank transfer to full fine-tuning [ 9 ] . A potential concern is that reducing σ A 2 \sigma_{A}^{2} might suppress the signal required for adaptation. In the fixed-rank setting below, the accumulated optimizer updates maintain the signal while Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] suppresses initialization noise.

chunks.section: Theorem 2 (Finite-Time Stability and Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] Efficiency (Informal)) .
chunks.text: In the fixed-rank setting of Theorem 1 , let t ≥ 2 t\geq 2 be finite, β , α / r = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \beta,\alpha/r=\Theta(1) , η A = Θ ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \eta_{A}=\Theta(n^{-1}) , and η B = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \eta_{B}=\Theta(1) . Assume C t ​ v t C_{t}v_{t} , C t ​ U A t ​ Z ¯ C_{t}U_{A}^{t}\underline{Z} , and U B t ​ v t U_{B}^{t}v_{t} have Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(n) coordinate magnitudes. Then Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] makes the initialization-dependent terms o ⁡ ( 1 ) o(1) while preserving Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \Theta(1) feature updates, and therefore satisfies the stability and efficiency conditions in Condition 1 . Standard Init[A] guarantees bounded feature updates, but a non-degenerate lower bound additionally requires a non-cancellation condition. The proof is given in Section A.3 . Under Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] , the initialization noise satisfies E N t = Θ ⁡ ( n − 1 ) E_{N}^{t}=\Theta(n^{-1}) , whereas the learned signal remains E S t = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) E_{S}^{t}=\Theta(1) . Hence the signal dominates and E total t / E S t → 1 E_{\mathrm{total}}^{t}/E_{S}^{t}\to 1 . Under standard Init[A] , both components can remain Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \Theta(1) , so the total feature norm is bounded but may become small through cancellation. Thus Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] guarantees non-degenerate feature learning under the stated assumptions, whereas Init[A] requires an additional non-cancellation assumption.

A recently proposed alternative, Init[AB] [ 34 ] , seeks to improve robustness by initializing both matrices with Θ ( n − 1 / 2 ) \Theta(n^{-1/2}) scaling and employing symmetric LRs η A = η B = Θ ( n − 1 / 2 ) \eta_{A}=\eta_{B}=\Theta(n^{-1/2}) . While this approach balances the global update norm, it inadvertently compromises the stability of the low-rank bottleneck: it fails to constrain the internal LoRA features Z A Z_{A} to Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \Theta(1) , leading to feature explosion in the large-width limit. For stable feature learning, it is crucial that not only the final output Z B Z_{B} but also the intermediate representation Z A Z_{A} evolves at a rate independent of the model width n n . Consider the update to the internal feature Δ ​ Z A t \Delta Z_{A}^{t} : Δ ​ Z A t = ( A t + 1 − A t ) ​ Z ¯ = − η A ​ U A t ​ Z ¯ . \Delta Z_{A}^{t}=(A_{t+1}-A_{t})\underline{Z}=-\eta_{A}U_{A}^{t}\underline{Z}. By the assumed alignment between the processed A A -update and the input, U A t ​ Z ¯ U_{A}^{t}\underline{Z} has Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(n) coordinate size in the low-rank dimension. Consequently, the magnitude of the internal feature shift scales as: ‖ Δ ​ Z A t ‖ 2 ∝ η A ⋅ n . \|\Delta Z_{A}^{t}\|_{2}\propto\eta_{A}\cdot n.

Under the Init[AB] regime where η A = Θ ( n − 1 / 2 ) \eta_{A}=\Theta(n^{-1/2}) , the internal update scales as Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(\sqrt{n}) , leading to feature updates that explode with model width. In contrast, both the standard Init[A] and our proposed Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] adopt the asymmetric scaling η A = Θ ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \eta_{A}=\Theta(n^{-1}) . This choice ensures ‖ Δ ​ Z A t ‖ 2 = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \|\Delta Z_{A}^{t}\|_{2}=\Theta(1) , maintaining stable feature evolution within the interaction bottleneck. We postulate that this key difference, preserving internal stability, is essential for consistent performance across varying model scales, a hypothesis supported by the empirical analysis in Figure 1 and subsequent experiments. In Sections E.1 and E.2 , experimental results demonstrate that Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] outperforms Init[AB] in most configurations, even under the condition η A = η B \eta_{A}=\eta_{B} . Moreover, Init[AB] exhibits notable performance degradation for large values of β \beta . The analysis above is deliberately stated through the signal-noise decomposition of the LoRA feature dynamics, because this decomposition isolates the initialization-dependent term that causes high-ratio instability. A complementary view is given in Section A.5 , where the spectral condition for feature learning [ 58 ] leads to the same Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] scaling by controlling the worst-case spectral norm. Section A.6 explains why γ \gamma -calculus can miss aligned directions in which the random initialization is amplified, and why the spectral condition again points to the Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] variance scaling σ A 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n − 2 ) \sigma_{A}^{2}=\Theta(n^{-2}) as the choice that makes the initialization noise asymptotically subdominant.

We evaluate whether Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] improves HP transfer and robustness in two settings: a controlled toy MLP and LLM fine-tuning. The LLM experiments cover both encoder-only models (RoBERTa-base on GLUE) and decoder-only models (Llama arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks, with additional backbones in the appendix). Across experiments, we vary the initialization scale β \beta , LR ratio η B / η A \eta_{B}/\eta_{A} , adapter rank r r , and LoRA multiplier α / r \alpha/r ; Init[A] uses base variance σ A 2 = 1 / n \sigma_{A}^{2}=1/n and Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] uses σ A 2 = 1 / n 2 \sigma_{A}^{2}=1/n^{2} , both with B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 . Full training details are in Appendix C .
Figure 3 : HP transfer on the MNIST toy example, measured by validation loss across widths and LRs.

To test HP transfer under Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] , we consider a simplified MLP equipped with LoRA ( α / r = 1 \alpha/r=1 ) on MNIST [ 31 ] : Y = W out ​ ℱ ​ ( ( W 0 + B ​ A ) , ℱ ⁡ ( W in , X ) ) , Y=W_{\text{out}}\mathcal{F}((W_{0}+BA),\mathcal{F}(W_{\text{in}},X)), where W in ∈ ℝ n × d W_{\text{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} , W out ∈ ℝ 10 × n W_{\text{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{10\times n} , W 0 ∈ ℝ n × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} , A ∈ ℝ r × n A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} , and B ∈ ℝ n × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} . Here ℱ ⁡ ( W , z ) = ReLU ⁡ ( W ​ z ) \mathcal{F}(W,z)=\operatorname{ReLU}(Wz) . We fix W 0 = 0 W_{0}=0 and freeze W in W_{\text{in}} and W out W_{\text{out}} after the μ \mu P initializations ( W out ) i ​ j ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , n − 2 ) (W_{\text{out}})_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,n^{-2}) and ( W in ) i ​ j ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) (W_{\text{in}})_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) [ 55 ] . To isolate the clean non-EMA normalized-update regime from our theory, we disable optimizer momentum and moving averages. We compare Init[A] and Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] across n ∈ { 16 , 64 , 256 , 1024 , 4096 } n\in\{16,64,256,1024,4096\} with a fixed LR ratio η B = n ​ η A \eta_{B}=n\eta_{A} and η A ∈ { 2 − 7 , ⋯ , 2 0 } \eta_{A}\in\{2^{-7},\cdots,2^{0}\} . For each width, we report the best validation loss over the LR grid, averaged over three seeds, and track the squared norms of the internal feature Z A Z_{A} and LoRA feature Z B Z_{B} to assess stability.

Figure 3 illustrates the HP transfer capabilities. At a low initialization scale ( β = 1.0 \beta=1.0 ), both methods exhibit consistent optimal LRs across widths. However, at a larger scale ( β = 5.0 \beta=5.0 ), the optimal LR for Init[A] drifts significantly at the largest width ( n = 4096 n=4096 ), and convergence degrades. In contrast, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] maintains stable HP transfer and achieves consistently lower validation loss, with the performance gap widening as β \beta increases. This stability is further corroborated by the feature norm evolution ( Figure 1 ), where Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] preserves the stability of Z A Z_{A} while the evolution of Z B Z_{B} is not affected by β \beta .

Figure 4 : Llama generation results. (a) Llama 3-8B with varying initialization scale β \beta . (b) Llama 3.2-1B with varying rank r r . Each panel reports arithmetic and commonsense accuracy under standard Init[A] and Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] while sweeping the LR ratio ρ = η B / η A \rho=\eta_{B}/\eta_{A} , implemented by fixing η A = 10 − 5 \eta_{A}=10^{-5} and setting η B = ρ ​ η A \eta_{B}=\rho\eta_{A} . Numerical labels mark endpoint ratios and near-optimal settings. Figure 5 : Final training loss reached during one epoch on the math benchmark. The LoRA multiplier is fixed to α / r = 1 \alpha/r=1 . (a) varies rank r r , and (b) varies initialization scale β \beta . The figure includes equal-LR sweeps with η = η A = η B \eta=\eta_{A}=\eta_{B} and LR-ratio sweeps; in the ratio panels, η A = 10 − 5 \eta_{A}=10^{-5} and η B = ρ ​ η A \eta_{B}=\rho\eta_{A} for ρ = η B / η A \rho=\eta_{B}/\eta_{A} .

To validate the effectiveness of our theory for real LLMs, we evaluate both encoder-only and decoder-only LLMs. We use RoBERTa on GLUE for encoder-only results, deferred to Section D.1 . For decoder-only generation, we fine-tune Llama 3-8B and Llama 3.2-1B [ 15 ] on arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks [ 23 ] , following the evaluation by Li et al. [34] : 10k arithmetic/math examples and 170k commonsense examples. For Llama 3-8B, we set r = α = 8 r=\alpha=8 and sweep β ∈ { 0.25 , 0.5 , 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } \beta\in\{0.25,0.5,1,2,4,8\} and ρ = η B / η A ∈ { 1 , 10 , 200 , 500 , 1000 , 2000 , 4000 } \rho=\eta_{B}/\eta_{A}\in\{1,10,200,500,1000,2000,4000\} , fixing η A = 10 − 5 \eta_{A}=10^{-5} and η B = ρ ​ η A \eta_{B}=\rho\eta_{A} . For Llama 3.2-1B, we fix β = 1 \beta=1 , sweep r ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 } r\in\{4,8,16,32,64,128\} , and set α = r \alpha=r . The loss study trains one epoch on math while varying r r , β \beta , equal LRs, and LR ratios.

Figure 4 shows that Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] is much less sensitive to β \beta and rank than standard Init[A] : it keeps broad high-accuracy regions across LR ratios, while Init[A] drifts toward smaller ratios and collapses at high ratios as β \beta or r r increases. The training-loss sweep in Figure 5 is consistent with the component decomposition. Here, β \beta appears explicitly only in the initialization term; the signal can still depend on β \beta indirectly through the optimizer trajectory. Empirically, the equal-LR optimum and best loss remain nearly unchanged across β \beta under Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] , consistent with suppression of initialization noise. However, because r r appears in both the signal and noise terms, the optimum LR also shifts for Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] when sweeping r r . Standard Init[A] does not suppress the noise, so its low-loss region narrows or shifts. In the ratio sweep, some drift can still appear because very large η B \eta_{B} can introduce its own stability issue, but Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] remains broader and more robust. The same qualitative pattern holds for encoder-only RoBERTa and for additional decoder-only Llama, Qwen, and Mistral backbones in Sections D.1 and 12 .

In both the analysis and experiments, we set the multiplier α / r = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \alpha/r=\Theta(1) . When this multiplier increases, it can also amplify initialization noise. This explains why many LoRA studies use relatively modest multipliers, often with α / r ≤ 2 \alpha/r\leq 2 [ 22 , 12 , 5 ] . However, a larger multiplier gives the learned low-rank update more influence on the model output and may therefore increase adaptability on hard decoder-only fine-tuning tasks. Our analysis suggests that the obstacle is not only stronger adaptation: α / r \alpha/r also amplifies the same initialization-dependent noise as β \beta ( Lemma 1 ). If this random-initialization effect is suppressed, larger multipliers need not be intrinsically unstable and may further improve performance. We therefore fix β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 , η A = 10 − 5 \eta_{A}=10^{-5} , and η B = 2 × 10 − 3 \eta_{B}=2\times 10^{-3} on Llama 3-8B arithmetic fine-tuning, then vary α / r \alpha/r .

Figure 6 : Arithmetic accuracy as the LoRA multiplier α / r \alpha/r increases. Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] remains stable at larger multipliers, while Init[A] degrades beyond α / r = 3 \alpha/r=3 . Figure 6 reveals a sharp stability gap. Init[A] peaks at α / r = 3 \alpha/r=3 (76.4%) and drops to 72.0% at α / r = 12 \alpha/r=12 , whereas Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] improves up to α / r = 10 \alpha/r=10 (77.5%) and remains stable at α / r = 12 \alpha/r=12 (77.3%). This matches our analysis: larger α / r \alpha/r amplifies both signal and noise, but Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] suppresses the initialization-dependent noise enough to exploit stronger low-rank updates without destabilizing the update from the signal term. Thus, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] makes tuning the multiplier α / r \alpha/r a viable way to further improve arithmetic fine-tuning performance. Five-seed multiplier validation, matched LR retuning, and longer-horizon comparisons are in Sections D.5 and D.4 .

We propose Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] , a simple LoRA initialization that suppresses initialization-induced noise while preserving zero initial adapter output. The central mechanism is that standard Init[A] leaves a random initial projection in A A that is amplified as soon as B B moves; Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] reduces this term by one additional factor of width, making high-ratio asymmetric LRs much less brittle. Practically, this reduces best-ratio drift across initialization scales, lowers dependence on exhaustive HP sweeps, and improves robustness to large update multipliers ( α / r ) (\alpha/r) , enabling stronger updates and better performance on downstream tasks. These gains are consistent across the controlled HP-transfer experiment, encoder-only RoBERTa fine-tuning, and decoder-only LLM generation benchmarks. More broadly, the design philosophy only targets the scale of A 0 A_{0} rather than its distribution. It can therefore be applied to structured initializers: we compress the A 0 A_{0} scale of Orthogonal and EVA while retaining their selected directions, and use a factorwise gauge transformation for PiSSA that preserves its initialized low-rank product. In selected Llama arithmetic sweeps, these three variance-compressed variants remain stable under aggressive asymmetric LRs for which their uncompressed counterparts degrade ( Section E.3 ). This extension is empirical: the B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 theorem does not directly cover PiSSA, and we do not claim uniform gains over carefully tuned base initializers.

Several limitations remain. Although some configurations are replicated across three to five seeds, most LR-ratio sweeps are single runs because of computational constraints, so small score differences in those sweeps should not be overinterpreted. Our empirical evaluation focuses on supervised fine-tuning of LLMs; extending the study to reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, broader generative-model training, and other adaptation settings is an important next step. Although Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] makes asymmetric LRs more robust and our analysis identifies factors that can shift the preferred ratio, including β \beta , r r , and α / r \alpha/r , we do not provide a direct rule for setting η B / η A \eta_{B}/\eta_{A} across arbitrary models and tasks. Developing such model-aware prescriptions, a fuller theory for rank r r and other LoRA HP interactions, and a better understanding of how far initialization scaling can be pushed beyond Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] are useful future directions. The limits of initialization scaling may connect to recent observations on the role of initialization in emergent reasoning behavior [ 61 ] .

When working with γ \gamma -calculus, we explicitly distinguish between Law of Large Numbers (LLN) and Central Limit Theorem (CLT) scaling. These two scaling regimes are fundamental in maximal-update-parameterization theory [ 56 ] , which enables HP transfer [ 55 ] . Here we give the two basic statistical rules and explain why they matter.

If X 1 , X 2 , ⋯ , X n X_{1},X_{2},\cdots,X_{n} are i.i.d. random variables with finite expected value 𝔼 ⁡ [ X i ] = μ \mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=\mu , then 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n X i → a.s. μ , as ​ n → ∞ . \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\mu,\quad\text{as }n\rightarrow\infty.

If X 1 , X 2 , ⋯ , X n X_{1},X_{2},\cdots,X_{n} are i.i.d. random variables with finite expected value 𝔼 ⁡ [ X i ] = μ \mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=\mu and finite variance Var ⁡ ( X i ) = σ 2 \operatorname{Var}(X_{i})=\sigma^{2} , then 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n ( X i − μ ) → 𝑑 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ) , as ​ n → ∞ . \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_{i}-\mu)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}),\quad\text{as }n\rightarrow\infty. These two statistical laws reveal two scenarios regarding the size of a sum of X i X_{i} when n n is large: ∑ i = 1 n X i ≈ n ​ μ ⏟ LLN + n ​ σ ​ 𝒩 ​ ( 0 , 1 ) ⏟ CLT . \sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\approx\underbrace{n\mu}_{\text{LLN}}+\underbrace{\sqrt{n}\sigma\mathcal{N}(0,1)}_{\text{CLT}}. For μ ≠ 0 \mu\neq 0 , | ∑ i = 1 n X i | / n → | μ | |\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}|/n\to|\mu| almost surely. For μ = 0 \mu=0 and 0 < σ 2 < ∞ 0<\sigma^{2}<\infty , the sum has RMS magnitude 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( ∑ i = 1 n X i ) 2 ] = σ ​ n \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i})^{2}]}=\sigma\sqrt{n} , but no deterministic lower bound follows.

In the scaling-limit theory of deep learning, we want to track the asymptotic behavior of key quantities such as LRs or initialization as we scale model ingredients such as width or depth. Prior work [ 18 , 17 , 34 ] uses γ \gamma -calculus to derive LoRA scaling rules with respect to the model width n n . If a variable v v has asymptotically polynomial magnitude in n n , i.e., | v | = Θ ⁡ ( n λ ) |v|=\Theta(n^{\lambda}) , we write λ = γ ⁡ [ v ] \lambda=\gamma[v] . Its exponent arithmetic follows these rules: • Zero: γ ⁡ [ 0 ] = − ∞ \gamma[0]=-\infty , corresponding to the limit γ ⁡ [ n λ ] \gamma[n^{\lambda}] when λ → − ∞ \lambda\rightarrow-\infty . • Product: For two real-valued variables v , v ′ ∈ ℝ v,v^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R} , we have γ ⁡ [ v ​ v ′ ] = γ ⁡ [ v ] + γ ⁡ [ v ′ ] \gamma[vv^{\prime}]=\gamma[v]+\gamma[v^{\prime}] . • Addition: Whenever the exponents exist, γ ⁡ [ v + v ′ ] ≤ max ⁡ ( γ ⁡ [ v ] , γ ⁡ [ v ′ ] ) \gamma[v+v^{\prime}]\leq\max(\gamma[v],\gamma[v^{\prime}]) . Equality holds if the exponents differ or | v + v ′ | = Θ ⁡ ( | v | + | v ′ | ) |v+v^{\prime}|=\Theta(|v|+|v^{\prime}|) ; excluding exact cancellation alone is insufficient.

chunks.section: A.5.1 Matrix Norm and Low-Rank Equivalence
chunks.text: The spectral norm of a matrix A A , denoted ∥ A ∥ op \lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{op}} , is its largest singular value, defined as the maximum stretch applied to any nonzero vector: ∥ A ∥ op = max v ≠ 0 ⁡ ∥ A ​ v ∥ 2 ∥ v ∥ 2 . \lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_{v\neq 0}\frac{\lVert Av\rVert_{2}}{\lVert v\rVert_{2}}. (9) The spectral norm can be bounded by the Frobenius norm: 1 / r ​ ∥ A ∥ F ≤ ∥ A ∥ op ≤ ∥ A ∥ F . 1/\sqrt{r}\lVert A\rVert_{F}\leq\lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\lVert A\rVert_{F}. (10) Here r ≥ 1 r\geq 1 is an upper bound on rank ⁡ ( A ) \operatorname{rank}(A) . In the fixed-rank LoRA setting of this subsection, the spectral and Frobenius norms are asymptotically equivalent: ∥ ⋅ ∥ F ≍ ∥ ⋅ ∥ op \lVert\cdot\rVert_{F}\asymp\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{op}} .

A central requirement for feature learning in large-width neural networks is that the feature representations must evolve nontrivially without vanishing or exploding. Following the feature-learning desiderata proposed by Yang et al. [57] , we start with the general condition for a weight matrix W ℓ ∈ ℝ n ℓ × n ℓ − 1 W_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times n_{\ell-1}} at layer ℓ \ell .

Consider applying a gradient update Δ ​ W ℓ ∈ ℝ n ℓ × n ℓ − 1 \Delta W_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times n_{\ell-1}} to the ℓ \ell -th weight matrix W ℓ W_{\ell} . To target the feature learning desideratum ‖ h ℓ ‖ 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n ℓ ) \|h_{\ell}\|_{2}=\Theta(\sqrt{n_{\ell}}) and ‖ Δ ​ h ℓ ‖ 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n ℓ ) \|\Delta h_{\ell}\|_{2}=\Theta(\sqrt{n_{\ell}}) , we use the spectral scaling prescription: ‖ W ℓ ‖ op = Θ ⁡ ( n ℓ n ℓ − 1 ) and ‖ Δ ​ W ℓ ‖ op = Θ ⁡ ( n ℓ n ℓ − 1 ) , for all layers ​ ℓ . \|W_{\ell}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\Theta\left(\sqrt{\frac{n_{\ell}}{n_{\ell-1}}}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad\|\Delta W_{\ell}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\Theta\left(\sqrt{\frac{n_{\ell}}{n_{\ell-1}}}\right),\quad\text{for all layers }\ell. (11) This condition controls the maximum amplification of an input signal. Matching lower bounds for realized features and their updates additionally require alignment and non-cancellation; spectral norms alone do not exclude inputs in a nullspace.

In the context of LoRA, we identify two distinct linear transformations: the down-projection A ∈ ℝ r × n A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} and the up-projection B ∈ ℝ n × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} . For the down-projection A A , we have n ℓ − 1 = n n_{\ell-1}=n and n ℓ = r n_{\ell}=r . Substituting these into Condition 2 and noting that r = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) r=\Theta(1) , we require: ∥ A ∥ op = Θ ( r n ) = Θ ( n − 1 / 2 ) . \|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\Theta\left(\sqrt{\frac{r}{n}}\right)=\Theta(n^{-1/2}). Conversely, for the up-projection B B , we have n ℓ − 1 = r n_{\ell-1}=r and n ℓ = n n_{\ell}=n . This yields the requirement: ‖ B ‖ op = Θ ⁡ ( n r ) = Θ ⁡ ( n 1 / 2 ) . \|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\Theta\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{r}}\right)=\Theta(n^{1/2}). The updates Δ ​ A \Delta A and Δ ​ B \Delta B require the same spectral scalings for stable feature evolution.

chunks.section: A.5.3 Implementing Feature Learning via Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ]
chunks.text: At fixed rank r = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) r=\Theta(1) , spectral and Frobenius norms have the same asymptotic scaling: ‖ A ‖ op ≍ ‖ A ‖ F \|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\asymp\|A\|_{F} . We therefore derive initialization variances and LRs from Frobenius norms. For an Adam-like optimizer, we model typical update entries as ( Δ ​ A ) i ​ j ∼ η A (\Delta A)_{ij}\sim\eta_{A} and ( Δ ​ B ) i ​ j ∼ η B (\Delta B)_{ij}\sim\eta_{B} .

chunks.section: Derivation for block A A ( A ∈ ℝ r × n A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} ).
chunks.text: The spectral condition mandates that the Frobenius norm squared scales as ‖ A ‖ F 2 ≍ ‖ A ‖ op 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \|A\|_{F}^{2}\asymp\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}=\Theta(n^{-1}) . With A 0 = β ​ A ~ 0 A_{0}=\beta\tilde{A}_{0} , β = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \beta=\Theta(1) , and independent centered Gaussian entries of variance σ A 2 \sigma_{A}^{2} in A ~ 0 \tilde{A}_{0} , the expected squared Frobenius norm is 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ A 0 ‖ F 2 ] = β 2 ​ r ​ n ​ σ A 2 \mathbb{E}[\|A_{0}\|_{F}^{2}]=\beta^{2}rn\sigma_{A}^{2} . At fixed rank, ‖ A 0 ‖ F 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n ​ σ A 2 ) \|A_{0}\|_{F}^{2}=\Theta(n\sigma_{A}^{2}) with high probability. Matching this to Θ ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \Theta(n^{-1}) gives σ A 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n − 2 ) \sigma_{A}^{2}=\Theta(n^{-2}) . Similarly, under the assumed update-entry scaling, ‖ Δ ​ A ‖ F 2 ≈ r ​ n ​ η A 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n ​ η A 2 ) \|\Delta A\|_{F}^{2}\approx rn\eta_{A}^{2}=\Theta(n\eta_{A}^{2}) . To satisfy ‖ Δ ​ A ‖ F 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \|\Delta A\|_{F}^{2}=\Theta(n^{-1}) , we set η A = Θ ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \eta_{A}=\Theta(n^{-1}) .

chunks.section: Derivation for block B B ( B ∈ ℝ n × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} ).
chunks.text: For the up-projection matrix, the spectral condition requires ‖ B ‖ F 2 ≍ ‖ B ‖ op 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n ) \|B\|_{F}^{2}\asymp\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}=\Theta(n) . Following the same logic, if B 0 B_{0} were initialized with variance σ B 2 \sigma_{B}^{2} , the expected norm would be 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ B 0 ‖ F 2 ] = n ​ r ​ σ B 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n ​ σ B 2 ) \mathbb{E}[\|B_{0}\|_{F}^{2}]=nr\sigma_{B}^{2}=\Theta(n\sigma_{B}^{2}) . Matching this to Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(n) implies σ B 2 = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \sigma_{B}^{2}=\Theta(1) . While standard LoRA initializes B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 , this transient violation is corrected in the first step provided the updates are properly scaled. For the updates, ‖ Δ ​ B ‖ F 2 ≈ n ​ r ​ η B 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n ​ η B 2 ) \|\Delta B\|_{F}^{2}\approx nr\eta_{B}^{2}=\Theta(n\eta_{B}^{2}) . To achieve the target Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(n) scaling, we require n ​ η B 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n ) n\eta_{B}^{2}=\Theta(n) , which simplifies to η B = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \eta_{B}=\Theta(1) . The derivation above dictates the following HPs to satisfy the spectral conditions for stable feature learning: σ A 2 = Θ ⁡ ( n − 2 ) \sigma_{A}^{2}=\Theta(n^{-2}) with η A = Θ ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \eta_{A}=\Theta(n^{-1}) , and by extension η B = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \eta_{B}=\Theta(1) . This configuration corresponds to our proposed Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] strategy, using Θ ⁡ ( n − 2 ) \Theta(n^{-2}) variance for the down-projection rather than the standard Θ ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \Theta(n^{-1}) scale. It controls spectral magnitudes; non-degenerate feature learning additionally requires the alignment and non-cancellation assumptions stated above.

chunks.section: A.6 Spectral Conditions for Robust LoRA Feature Learning
chunks.text: Prior work [ 18 , 17 , 34 ] provides useful intuition for LoRA scaling, but its coordinate-wise, average-case γ \gamma -calculus can obscure a failure mode in practical fine-tuning. We explain how a spectral, worst-case perspective [ 57 ] leads to the Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] scaling.

chunks.section: A.6.1 Why γ \gamma -Calculus Is Not Sufficient
chunks.text: The γ \gamma -calculus tracks the coordinate-wise magnitude of random variables. The framework is implicitly average-case, assuming that summations exhibit typical cancellations and that individual coordinates are representative of global behavior. This assumption leads to fundamental limitations. For a matrix-vector product W ​ x Wx , the scaling also depends on cancellation among the products W i ​ j ​ x j W_{ij}x_{j} . Under suitable independence and moment assumptions, two benchmark rules are: • CLT-like (centered summands): γ ⁡ [ W ​ x ] = γ ⁡ [ W ] + γ ⁡ [ x ] + 1 / 2 \gamma[Wx]=\gamma[W]+\gamma[x]+1/2 • LLN-like (nonzero-mean summands): γ ⁡ [ W ​ x ] = γ ⁡ [ W ] + γ ⁡ [ x ] + 1 \gamma[Wx]=\gamma[W]+\gamma[x]+1 Neither rule follows from the marginal mean of W W alone when W W and x x are dependent. In LoRA, the initialization-dependent and optimizer-driven components can have different rank contractions, as captured by γ N \gamma_{N} and γ S \gamma_{S} in Theorem 1 . Tracking only the final feature’s coordinate exponent does not distinguish these components or their signed cross term. The explicit decomposition is therefore needed to diagnose noise dominance even when the total feature satisfies a bounded scaling condition.
Following Yang et al. [57] , the worst-case spectral condition is:

Conversely, ‖ B ‖ op = Θ ⁡ ( n 1 / 2 ) \|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\Theta(n^{1/2}) maps an aligned order-one bottleneck vector to output scale Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(\sqrt{n}) . These worst-case scales do not by themselves give lower bounds for arbitrary inputs. By Lemma 1 , T noise t = − ( α ​ β / r ) ​ η B ​ ( ∑ i < t U B i ) ​ A ~ 0 ​ Z ¯ T_{\text{noise}}^{t}=-(\alpha\beta/r)\eta_{B}(\sum_{i<t}U_{B}^{i})\tilde{A}_{0}\underline{Z} . At fixed rank, coordinate-bounded directions give ‖ ∑ i < t U B i ‖ op = O ⁡ ( t ​ n ) \|\sum_{i<t}U_{B}^{i}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(t\sqrt{n}) , while Gaussian initialization gives ‖ A ~ 0 ‖ op = Θ ⁡ ( σ A ​ n ) \|\tilde{A}_{0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\Theta(\sigma_{A}\sqrt{n}) with high probability. Therefore the worst-case noise RMS satisfies

chunks.section: Condition 3 (Spectral Condition for LoRA Feature Learning) .
chunks.text: ‖ T noise t ‖ 2 n = O ⁡ ( α ​ β r ​ η B ​ t ​ σ A ​ n ) . \frac{\|T_{\text{noise}}^{t}\|_{2}}{\sqrt{n}}=O\!\left(\frac{\alpha\beta}{r}\eta_{B}t\sigma_{A}n\right). For fixed t t and α / r , β , η B = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \alpha/r,\beta,\eta_{B}=\Theta(1) , this bound is O ⁡ ( n ) O(\sqrt{n}) under Init[A] and O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) under Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] . Thus the spectral argument establishes bounded worst-case noise RMS for Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] , but does not establish vanishing noise or signal dominance for all aligned inputs. Vanishing noise and signal dominance require the fixed-input projection and contraction assumptions in Theorems 1 and 2 ; we derive the spectral initialization rule in Section A.5 .

Standard LoRA sets B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 and initializes A 0 A_{0} with mean-zero entries of variance Θ ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \Theta(n^{-1}) , denoted Init[A] ; PEFT uses Kaiming-uniform initialization ( Section C.1 ). Hayou et al. [18] show that the symmetric configuration Init[B] , with A 0 = 0 A_{0}=0 and B 0 B_{0} initialized at entrywise variance Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \Theta(1) , has inferior optimization dynamics and stability compared with Init[A] . PEFT [ 40 ] also offers initialization strategies to accelerate convergence or enhance stability. LoftQ [ 36 ] minimizes the quantization error between original and quantized weights. PiSSA [ 42 ] and EVA [ 44 ] adopt spectral approaches: PiSSA uses principal singular components of the weight matrix to approximate full-rank updates, while EVA uses a singular value decomposition of layer input activations. CorDA [ 59 ] uses context-oriented decomposition to preserve world knowledge or enhance task-specific learning. OLoRA [ 8 ] and orthogonal initialization use orthonormal decompositions for stable training.

Beyond initialization, LoRA introduces sensitivity to several coupled HPs, including the rank r r , scaling factor α \alpha , and LRs η A , η B \eta_{A},\eta_{B} . The rank controls the expressivity of the adapter: Zeng and Lee [60] characterize the expressive power of low-rank adaptation and clarify how the choice of r r constrains the class of attainable updates. However, increasing rank does not automatically improve vanilla LoRA. Kalajdzievski [27] show that the conventional multiplier α / r \alpha/r can make the LoRA branch weaker as r r grows, so higher ranks may yield diminishing gains in practice. Their rank-stabilized alternative replaces this scaling with α / r \alpha/\sqrt{r} , preserving a more consistent update scale across ranks.

LR selection introduces a separate source of brittleness. In the feature-learning view, useful transfer requires both the hidden states and their updates to remain Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \Theta(1) as width increases. Hayou et al. [17] analyze LoRA in the infinite-width limit and derive stability conditions under which non-degenerate feature updates require a large LR separation, with η B ≫ η A \eta_{B}\gg\eta_{A} and an idealized ratio that scales with width. Recent work further studies the joint width-and-rank limit, showing that optimal LR-rank scaling depends on the initialization and LoRA update multiplier [ 9 ] . These theories provide guidance, but pretrained LLMs typically do not use the corresponding width-scaling parameterization. Empirical studies find that vanilla LoRA can be competitive after careful LR search [ 32 ] , while the best asymmetric LR ratios observed in practice are often far smaller than the model width [ 17 ] . We address this theory-to-practice gap through initialization: standard Init[A] injects persistent noise under aggressive asymmetric LRs, whereas Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] suppresses it and improves robustness.

chunks.section: B.3 Feature Learning and HP Transfer
chunks.text: Feature learning [ 56 ] is a central mechanism in modern deep learning, wherein neural networks are trained not merely to match target outputs, but to acquire internal representations that encode useful invariances and hierarchical abstractions. This stands in contrast to the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) or “lazy” training regime [ 24 , 1 , 37 ] , in which an infinite-width network behaves as a kernel machine with features effectively frozen at their random initialization. In the feature-learning regime, by contrast, the network’s internal feature map evolves substantially over the course of training. To facilitate scalable feature learning, Yang and Hu [56] introduced the maximal update parametrization ( μ \mu P), which enables nontrivial feature-learning dynamics even in the infinite-width limit. Unlike the NTK parametrization, μ \mu P ensures that pre-activations, gradients, and parameter updates remain Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \Theta(1) as the network width tends to infinity. Closely related approaches based on mean-field theory [ 10 , 41 , 47 ] likewise analyze the evolution of the distribution of neurons and demonstrate that learned features can emerge outside the kernel regime. While early scaling analyses focused on width, recent work has extended these ideas to the depth scaling limit, where the number of layers L → ∞ L\to\infty . Naively deep networks are prone to vanishing activations or exploding gradients, but these issues can be resolved by scaling residual blocks as O ⁡ ( 1 / L ) O(1/\sqrt{L}) [ 58 , 7 ] .

chunks.section: B.3 Feature Learning and HP Transfer
chunks.text: A key use case is HP transfer across model scales [ 55 ] . Because μ \mu P maintains consistent training dynamics across width and depth, practitioners can tune LRs and other HPs on small proxy models for use in larger networks. Empirical methods [ 43 , 30 , 46 ] similarly normalize layer outputs and updates for width transfer. Related work studies transformer width-to-depth ratios [ 14 ] , sharpness-aware optimization [ 16 ] , sparse training [ 13 ] , and state space models [ 48 ] .

While feature learning offers insight into representation adaptation, such analyses typically depend on a specific choice of parameterization to guarantee well-behaved limits as network width grows. However, not all models are parameterized in this manner, and identifying an appropriate parameterization can be challenging for complex architectures. This motivates a complementary line of research that elevates training stability to a primary objective, often treated as orthogonal to, or only weakly coupled with, feature-learning optimality. Historically, stability concerns were most prominent in recurrent neural networks, where unconstrained temporal composition of states led to exploding or vanishing gradients. Architectures such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) [ 20 ] and Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) [ 11 ] mitigated these issues by introducing gated, additive state updates that constrain the hidden dynamics to a contractive, well-conditioned manifold, thereby enabling stable gradient propagation over long time horizons. From a geometric perspective, these mechanisms effectively bound the recurrent Jacobian and attenuate sensitivity to HPs. Muon [ 26 ] and the Spectral Sphere Optimizer [ 51 ] constrain optimization trajectories to spectrally controlled manifolds, regulating operator norms for stability. Layer Normalization [ 2 ] , Post-LN Transformers [ 50 ] , and Pre-LN Transformers [ 53 ] can also be interpreted as imposing implicit spectral control. DeepSeek’s manifold hyperconnections [ 52 ] constrain learned residual mixing matrices to the doubly stochastic manifold, yielding convex, well-conditioned layer compositions.

For transformer fine-tuning (RoBERTa, Llama, Qwen, and Mistral), we follow the PEFT convention [ 40 ] : Kaiming-uniform A A [ 19 ] and B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 . [34] apply the γ \gamma -calculus to derive another initialization strategy, Init[AB] , that can be more robust to suboptimal LRs. The robustness is attributed to the condition: γ ⁡ [ A 0 ] + γ ⁡ [ B 0 ] = − 1 . \gamma[A_{0}]+\gamma[B_{0}]=-1. Strictly speaking, since B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 , γ ⁡ [ B 0 ] = − ∞ \gamma[B_{0}]=-\infty under the γ \gamma -calculus convention. The relevant comparison is instead with the first nonzero B B update, whose target/update scale under η B = Θ ⁡ ( 1 ) \eta_{B}=\Theta(1) is γ ⁡ [ Δ ​ B ] = 0 \gamma[\Delta B]=0 . Thus Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] attains the desired post-update scaling, γ ⁡ [ A 0 ] = − 1 \gamma[A_{0}]=-1 and γ ⁡ [ Δ ​ B ] = 0 \gamma[\Delta B]=0 , with zero initial adapter output. Its two advantages over Init[AB] are: 1. Internal Stability : Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] maintains bounded internal features Z A Z_{A} , preventing the feature explosion characteristic of Init[AB] ( Figure 1 ) 2. Implementation Efficiency : Unlike Init[AB] , which necessitates nonzero initialization for both matrices and subsequent weight subtraction to preserve the pretrained mapping, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] allows B = 0 B=0 . This simplifies implementation and avoids inference overhead.

To validate these advantages, we compare the two strategies on SST-2 and MNLI across varying initialization scales β ∈ { 0.25 , 0.5 , 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } \beta\in\{0.25,0.5,1,2,4,8\} and symmetric LRs η A = η B = η ∈ { 1 × 10 − 5 , 3 × 10 − 5 , 8 × 10 − 5 , 1 × 10 − 4 , 3 × 10 − 4 , 8 × 10 − 4 , 1 × 10 − 3 } \eta_{A}=\eta_{B}=\eta\in\{1\times 10^{-5},3\times 10^{-5},8\times 10^{-5},1\times 10^{-4},3\times 10^{-4},8\times 10^{-4},1\times 10^{-3}\} . We study LoRA initialization to improve the understanding and robustness of parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We identify no direct negative societal impacts unique to this initialization; broader impacts depend on the underlying pretrained models and their downstream uses.

We used large language models to polish the language and improve presentation clarity. We also use Codex to clean up the code and maintain the code base. The core research ideas, technical content, theoretical analysis, experimental design, and scientific conclusions were generated by the authors.

1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract and introduction state the proposed Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] initialization, the signal–noise mechanism, and the empirical claims. The analysis and experiments in the main paper and appendix support these claims within the stated assumptions and evaluated settings. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The conclusion discusses open limitations, including the focus on supervised fine-tuning, the lack of a direct rule for choosing asymmetric LR ratios across arbitrary models and tasks, the need for a fuller theory of other LoRA HPs such as rank r r , and the uncertainty around more aggressive initialization scaling. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

• The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs

Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The main text states the informal theorem assumptions, and the appendix provides the full decomposition, normalized-update assumptions, Adam/AdamW conditions, and proofs. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The experimental setup, datasets, model choices, LoRA HPs, optimizer settings, and sweep ranges are described in the main experiment section and in the experimental-details appendix. Reconstruction details and limitations are documented in the public experiment guide and Section C.2 . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general, releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

(c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The main text and appendix specify the benchmark tasks, models, LoRA modules, rank, scaling factor, LR sweeps, optimizers, batch sizes, sequence lengths, and training epochs. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance

Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [No] Justification: The appendix reports selected three- and five-seed accuracy summaries and confidence intervals, while most main language-understanding and generation heatmaps remain single-run. The reported uncertainty types and interval-construction methods are not yet fully documented. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

• If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The appendix reports the GPU type used for the experiments. Each individual fine-tuning run is relatively cheap and can be completed within roughly three hours on a single L40s GPU, but the full set of reported experiments requires substantially more total compute because we sweep many combinations of initialization scale, LR ratio, rank, and LoRA multiplier. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Answer: [Yes] Justification: The work studies initialization and optimization behavior for parameter-efficient fine-tuning and does not involve data collection from human subjects, unsafe data release, or intentionally harmful applications.
